# interpolator - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/interpolator/

## Expand description

Runtime implementation of [ format!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/macro.format.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#stdfmt-compatible-formatting)`std::fmt` compatible formatting

All options but the fill character for alignment is supported
(due to [rust-lang/rfcs#3394](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3394)).

Though the non [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) traits need to be enabled through

[features](https://docs.rs#features).

```
use interpolator::{format, Formattable};
let formatted = format(
    "{value:+05}", // could be dynamic
    &[("value", Formattable::display(&12))]
        .into_iter()
        .collect::<HashMap<_, _>>(),
)?;
assert_eq!(formatted, format!("{:+05}", 12));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#i-iter-format)`i` iter format

The feature `iter` enables an additional format trait `i`, it allows to
format a list of values with a format string and an optional join
expression.

The syntax is `{list:i(the format string, '{}' is the array element)(the join)}`, an empty join can also be omitted `{list:i({})}`. If join is omitted
the format string `{}` can be omitted as well `{list:i}`.

Should you need to use `)` inside your format string or join, you can add `#`
similar to rust’s [raw string](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/tokens.html#raw-string-literals)
(i.e. `#(({}))#`).

It is also possible to only iterate a sub-slice specified through a range
before the format string, i.e. `{list:i1..4}`. For open ranges range
bounds can also be omitted. To index from the end, you can use negative
range bounds.

It is also possible to index a single value by only specifying an `isize``{list:i1}`.

A [ Formattable](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html) implementing iter is created using

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html#method.iter)

`Formattable::iter````
// HashMap macro
use collection_literals::hash;
use interpolator::{format, Formattable};
// Needs to be a slice of references because `Formattable::display` expects a
// reference
let items = [&"hello", &"hi", &"hey"].map(Formattable::display);
let items = Formattable::iter(&items);
let format_str = "Greetings: {items:i..-1(`{}{outside}`)(, )} and `{items:i-1}{outside}`";
assert_eq!(
    format(format_str, &hash!("items" => items, "outside" => Formattable::display(&'!')))?,
    "Greetings: `hello!`, `hi!` and `hey!`"
);
```
See [ format()](https://docs.rs/fn.format.html) and

[for details.](https://docs.rs/fn.write.html)

`write()`[§](https://docs.rs#macros)Macros

To simplify creating contexts, some macros are provided.

- `context!`- `HashMap<&str, Formattable>`- `format()`
- `list!`- `Formattable`- [iter](https://docs.rs/%60i%60-iter-format).
- `iformat!`- `iwrite!`- `format()`- `write()`
- Most of std’s formatting macros are supported with an `i`prefix:

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

By default only [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) is supported, the rest of the

[formatting traits](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/index.html#formatting-traits)can be enabled through the following features.

- `debug`enables- `?`,- `x?`and- `X?`trait specifiers
- `number`enables- `x`,- `X`,- `b`,- `o`,- `e`and- `E`trait specifiers
- `pointer`enables- `p`trait specifiers
- `iter`enables- `i`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros-1)

- [context](https://docs.rs/macro.context.html)
- Creates a context for use with this crate’s `format()``write()`
- [ieprint](https://docs.rs/macro.ieprint.html)
- `eprint!`- `iformat!`
- [ieprintln](https://docs.rs/macro.ieprintln.html)
- `eprintln!`- `iformat!`
- [iformat](https://docs.rs/macro.iformat.html)
- `format()`
- [iprint](https://docs.rs/macro.iprint.html)
- `print!`- `iformat!`
- [iprintln](https://docs.rs/macro.iprintln.html)
- `println!`- `iformat!`
- [iwrite](https://docs.rs/macro.iwrite.html)
- `write()`
- [iwriteln](https://docs.rs/macro.iwriteln.html)
- Like `writeln!``write()`
- [list](https://docs.rs/macro.list.html)
- Creates a list of formattable values, applying th specified traits, or display if without a trait specifier.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Formattable](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html)
- Utility struct holding references to the trait implementation of a value to enable runtime verification and execution of them

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- Error returned by `format()`
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/enum.ParseError.html)- Error
- Error caused by invalid format string
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.Trait.html)
- The trait used to format.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Context](https://docs.rs/trait.Context.html)
- Context for `format`and`write`

## Expand description

# interpolator 0.5.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/interpolator/latest

# interpolator

Runtime implementation of `format!`.

`format`

Runtime version of `format!`.

Takes a string and a context, containing `Formattable` values, returns a
string.

```
use HashMap;
use ;
let formatted = format
.unwrap;
assert_eq!;
```
`write`

Runtime version of `write!`.

Takes a mutable `Write` e.g. `&mut String`, a format string and a context,
containing `Formattable` values.

```
use HashMap;
use ;

let mut buf = Stringnew;
write
.unwrap;

assert_eq!;
```
`i` iter format

The feature `iter` enables an additional format trait `i`, it allows to
format a list of values with a format string and an optional join
expression.

The syntax is `{list:i(the format string, '{}' is the array element)(the join)}`, an empty join can also be omitted `{list:i({})}`. If join is omitted
the format string `{}` can be omitted as well `{list:i}`.

Should you need to use `)` inside your format string or join, you can add `#`
similar to rust's [raw string](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/tokens.html#raw-string-literals)
(i.e. `#(({}))#`).

It is also possible to only iterate a sub-slice specified through a range
before the format string, i.e. `{list:i1..4}`. For open ranges range
bounds can also be omitted. To index from the end, you can use negative
range bounds.

It is also possible to index a single value by only specifying an `isize`
`{list:i1}`.

A `Formattable` implementing iter is created using `Formattable::iter`:

```
// HashMap macro
use hash;
use ;
// Needs to be a slice of references because `Formattable::display` expects a
// reference
let items = .map;
let items = iter;
let format_str = "Greetings: {items:i..-1(`{it}`)(, )} and {items:i-1..(`{it}`)}";
assert_eq!;
# return Ok::
```
# Features

By default only `Display` is supported, the rest of the
[formatting traits](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/index.html#formatting-traits)
can be enabled through the following features.

- `debug`enables- `?`,- `x?`and- `X?`trait specifiers
- `number`enables- `x`,- `X`,- `b`,- `o`,- `e`and- `E`trait specifiers
- `pointer`enables- `p`trait specifiers
- `iter`enables- `i`trait specifier

- Macro for initializing collections of any type.

# derive_more - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/derive_more/^0.99.17/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#derive_more)`derive_more`

Rust has lots of builtin traits that are implemented for its basic types, such
as `Add`, `Not`, `From` or `Display`.
However, when wrapping these types inside your own structs or enums you lose the
implementations of these traits and are required to recreate them.
This is especially annoying when your own structures are very simple, such as
when using the commonly advised newtype pattern (e.g. `MyInt(i32)`).

This library tries to remove these annoyances and the corresponding boilerplate code. It does this by allowing you to derive lots of commonly used traits for both structs and enums.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-code)Example code

By using this library the following code just works:

```
extern crate derive_more;
use derive_more::{Add, Display, From, Into};
#[derive(PartialEq, From, Add)]
struct MyInt(i32);
#[derive(PartialEq, From, Into)]
struct Point2D {
    x: i32,
    y: i32,
}
#[derive(PartialEq, From, Add, Display)]
enum MyEnum {
    #[display(fmt = "int: {}", _0)]
    Int(i32),
    Uint(u32),
    #[display(fmt = "nothing")]
    Nothing,
}
assert!(MyInt(11) == MyInt(5) + 6.into());
assert!((5, 6) == Point2D { x: 5, y: 6 }.into());
assert!(MyEnum::Int(15) == (MyEnum::Int(8) + 7.into()).unwrap());
assert!(MyEnum::Int(15).to_string() == "int: 15");
assert!(MyEnum::Uint(42).to_string() == "42");
assert!(MyEnum::Nothing.to_string() == "nothing");
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-derivable-traits)The derivable traits

Below are all the traits that you can derive using this library. Some trait derivations are so similar that the further documentation will only show a single one of them. You can recognize these by the “-like” suffix in their name. The trait name before that will be the only one that is used throughout the further documentation.

It is important to understand what code gets generated when using one of the derives from this crate. That is why the links below explain what code gets generated for a trait for each group from before.

You can use the [ cargo-expand](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-expand) utility to see the exact code that is generated
for your specific type.
This will show you your code with all macros and derives expanded.

**NOTE**: You still have to derive each trait separately. So `#[derive(Mul)]` doesn’t
automatically derive `Div` as well. To derive both you should do `#[derive(Mul, Div)]`

[§](https://docs.rs#conversion-traits)Conversion traits

These are traits that are used to convert automatically between types.

[§](https://docs.rs#formatting-traits)Formatting traits

These traits are used for converting a struct to a string in different ways.

- `Display`-like- `Display`,- `Binary`,- `Octal`,- `LowerHex`,- `UpperHex`,- `LowerExp`,- `UpperExp`,- `Pointer`

[§](https://docs.rs#error-handling-traits)Error-handling traits

These traits are used to define error-types.

[§](https://docs.rs#operators)Operators

These are traits that can be used for operator overloading.

- `Index`
- `Deref`
- `Not`-like- `Not`and- `Neg`
- `Add`-like- `Add`,- `Sub`,- `BitAnd`,- `BitOr`,- `BitXor`
- `Mul`-like- `Mul`,- `Div`,- `Rem`,- `Shr`and- `Shl`
- `Sum`-like- `Sum`and- `Product`
- `IndexMut`
- `DerefMut`
- `AddAssign`-like- `AddAssign`,- `SubAssign`,- `BitAndAssign`,- `BitOrAssign`and- `BitXorAssign`
- `MulAssign`-like- `MulAssign`,- `DivAssign`,- `RemAssign`,- `ShrAssign`and- `ShlAssign`

[§](https://docs.rs#static-methods)Static methods

These don’t derive traits, but derive static methods instead.

- `Constructor`- `new`method that can be used as a constructor. This is very basic if you need more customization for your constructor, check out the- `derive-new`
- `IsVariant`- `foo`of an enum type, derives a- `is_foo`method.
- `Unwrap`- `foo`of an enum type, derives an- `unwrap_foo`method.

[§](https://docs.rs#generated-code)Generated code

[§](https://docs.rs#installation)Installation

This library requires Rust 1.65 or higher and it supports `no_std` out of the box.
Then add the following to `Cargo.toml`:

```
[dependencies]
derive_more = "0.99.0"
# You can specifiy the types of derives that you need for less time spent
# compiling. For the full list of features see this crate its Cargo.toml.
default-features = false
features = ["from", "add", "iterator"]
```
And this to the top of your Rust file for Rust 2018:

```
extern crate derive_more;
// use the derives that you want in the file
use derive_more::{Add, Display, From};
```
If you’re still using Rust 2015 you should add this instead:

```
extern crate core;
#[macro_use]
extern crate derive_more;
```

# proptest - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/proptest/^1.1.0/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#proptest-reference-documentation)Proptest Reference Documentation

This is the reference documentation for the proptest API.

For documentation on how to get started with proptest and general usage
advice, please refer to the [Proptest Book](https://proptest-rs.github.io/proptest/intro.html).

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [arbitrary](https://docs.rs/arbitrary/index.html)
- Defines the `Arbitrary`trait and related free functions and type aliases.
- [array](https://docs.rs/array/index.html)
- Support for strategies producing fixed-length arrays.
- [bits](https://docs.rs/bits/index.html)
- Strategies for working with bit sets.
- [bool](https://docs.rs/bool/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `bool`values.
- [char](https://docs.rs/char/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `char`values.
- [collection](https://docs.rs/collection/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `std::collections`of values.
- [num](https://docs.rs/num/index.html)
- Strategies to generate numeric values (as opposed to integers used as bit fields).
- [option](https://docs.rs/option/index.html)
- Strategies for generating `std::Option`values.
- [path](https://docs.rs/path/index.html)- `std`
- Strategies for generating [`PathBuf`] and related path types.
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Re-exports the most commonly-needed APIs of proptest.
- [range_](https://docs.rs/range_subset/index.html)- subset - `std`
- Strategies for generating values by taking samples of index ranges.
- [result](https://docs.rs/result/index.html)
- Strategies for combining delegate strategies into `std::Result`s.
- [sample](https://docs.rs/sample/index.html)
- Strategies for generating values by taking samples of collections.
- [strategy](https://docs.rs/strategy/index.html)
- Defines the core traits used by Proptest.
- [string](https://docs.rs/string/index.html)- `std`
- Strategies for generating strings and byte strings from regular expressions.
- [test_](https://docs.rs/test_runner/index.html)- runner
- State and functions for running proptest tests.
- [tuple](https://docs.rs/tuple/index.html)
- Support for combining strategies into tuples.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assert.html)- assert
- Similar to `assert!`from std, but returns a test failure instead of panicking if the condition fails.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assert_eq.html)- assert_ - eq
- Similar to `assert_eq!`from std, but returns a test failure instead of panicking if the condition fails.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assert_ne.html)- assert_ - ne
- Similar to `assert_ne!`from std, but returns a test failure instead of panicking if the condition fails.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_assume.html)- assume
- Rejects the test input if assumptions are not met.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_compose.html)- compose
- Convenience to define functions which produce new strategies.
- [prop_](https://docs.rs/macro.prop_oneof.html)- oneof
- Produce a strategy which picks one of the listed choices.
- [proptest](https://docs.rs/macro.proptest.html)
- Easily define `proptest`tests.

## Attribute Macros[§](https://docs.rs#attributes)

- [property_](https://docs.rs/attr.property_test.html)- test - `attr-macro`
- The `property_test`procedural macro simplifies the creation of property-based tests using the`proptest`crate. This macro provides a more concise syntax for writing tests that automatically generate test cases based on properties.

# quote - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/quote/^1.0.23/

## Expand description

This crate provides the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for turning Rust syntax tree data
structures into tokens of source code.

Procedural macros in Rust receive a stream of tokens as input, execute arbitrary Rust code to determine how to manipulate those tokens, and produce a stream of tokens to hand back to the compiler to compile into the caller’s crate. Quasi-quoting is a solution to one piece of that — producing tokens to return to the compiler.

The idea of quasi-quoting is that we write *code* that we treat as *data*.
Within the `quote!` macro, we can write what looks like code to our text
editor or IDE. We get all the benefits of the editor’s brace matching,
syntax highlighting, indentation, and maybe autocompletion. But rather than
compiling that as code into the current crate, we can treat it as data, pass
it around, mutate it, and eventually hand it back to the compiler as tokens
to compile into the macro caller’s crate.

This crate is motivated by the procedural macro use case, but is a general-purpose Rust quasi-quoting library and is not specific to procedural macros.

```
[dependencies]
quote = "1.0"
```
[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

The following quasi-quoted block of code is something you might find in [a](https://serde.rs/)
procedural macro having to do with data structure serialization. The `#var`
syntax performs interpolation of runtime variables into the quoted tokens.
Check out the documentation of the [ quote!](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html) macro for more detail about
the syntax. See also the

[macro which is important for implementing hygienic procedural macros.](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)

`quote_spanned!````
let tokens = quote! {
    struct SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        value: &'a #field_ty,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData<#item_ty>,
    }
    impl #generics serde::Serialize for SerializeWith #generics #where_clause {
        fn serialize<S>(&self, serializer: S) -> Result<S::Ok, S::Error>
        where
            S: serde::Serializer,
        {
            #path(self.value, serializer)
        }
    }
    SerializeWith {
        value: #value,
        phantom: core::marker::PhantomData::<#item_ty>,
    }
};
```
[§](https://docs.rs#non-macro-code-generators)Non-macro code generators

When using `quote` in a build.rs or main.rs and writing the output out to a
file, consider having the code generator pass the tokens through
[prettyplease](https://github.com/dtolnay/prettyplease) before writing. This way if an error occurs in the generated
code it is convenient for a human to read and debug.

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros)

- [format_](https://docs.rs/macro.format_ident.html)- ident
- Formatting macro for constructing `Ident`s.
- [quote](https://docs.rs/macro.quote.html)
- The whole point.
- [quote_](https://docs.rs/macro.quote_spanned.html)- spanned
- Same as `quote!`, but applies a given span to all tokens originating within the macro invocation.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Ident](https://docs.rs/trait.IdentFragment.html)- Fragment
- Specialized formatting trait used by `format_ident!`.
- [ToTokens](https://docs.rs/trait.ToTokens.html)
- Types that can be interpolated inside a `quote!`invocation.
- [Token](https://docs.rs/trait.TokenStreamExt.html)- Stream - Ext
- TokenStream extension trait with methods for appending tokens.

---

# trybuild2 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/trybuild2/^1.0.0/

## Expand description

[![github]](https://github.com/GuillaumeGomez/trybuild2) [![crates-io]](https://crates.io/crates/trybuild2) [![docs-rs]](https://docs.rs/trybuild2)

`trybuild2` is a fork of [trybuild](https://github.com/dtolnay/trybuild)
which allows to have inline tests.

[§](https://docs.rs#a-compiler-diagnostics-testing-library-in-just-3-functions) A compiler diagnostics testing library in just 3 functions.

Trybuild2 is a test harness for invoking rustc on a set of test cases and asserting that any resulting error messages are the ones intended.

Such tests are commonly useful for testing error reporting involving procedural macros. We would write test cases triggering either errors detected by the macro or errors detected by the Rust compiler in the resulting expanded code, and compare against the expected errors to ensure that they remain user-friendly.

This style of testing is sometimes called *ui tests* because they test
aspects of the user’s interaction with a library outside of what would be
covered by ordinary API tests.

Nothing here is specific to macros; trybuild2 would work equally well for testing misuse of non-macro APIs.

[§](https://docs.rs#compile-fail-tests)Compile-fail tests

A minimal trybuild2 setup looks like this:

```
#[test]
fn ui() {
    let t = trybuild2::TestCases::new();
    t.compile_fail("tests/ui/*.rs");
}
```
The test can be run with `cargo test`. It will individually compile each of
the source files matching the glob pattern, expect them to fail to compile,
and assert that the compiler’s error message matches an adjacently named
**.stderr* file containing the expected output (same file name as the test
except with a different extension). If it matches, the test case is
considered to succeed.

Dependencies listed under `[dev-dependencies]` in the project’s Cargo.toml
are accessible from within the test cases.

Failing tests display the expected vs actual compiler output inline.

A compile_fail test that fails to fail to compile is also a failure.

[§](https://docs.rs#pass-tests)Pass tests

The same test harness is able to run tests that are expected to pass, too.
Ordinarily you would just have Cargo run such tests directly, but being able
to combine modes like this could be useful for workshops in which
participants work through test cases enabling one at a time. Trybuild was
originally developed for my [procedural macros workshop at Rust
Latam](https://github.com/dtolnay/proc-macro-workshop).

```
#[test]
fn ui() {
    let t = trybuild2::TestCases::new();
    t.pass("tests/01-parse-header.rs");
    t.pass("tests/02-parse-body.rs");
    t.compile_fail("tests/03-expand-four-errors.rs");
    t.pass("tests/04-paste-ident.rs");
    t.pass("tests/05-repeat-section.rs");
    //t.pass("tests/06-make-work-in-function.rs");
    //t.pass("tests/07-init-array.rs");
    //t.compile_fail("tests/08-ident-span.rs");
    t.compile_fail_inline("name", "fn main() {}", "path-to-stderr");
    t.compile_fail_check_sub("tests/03-expand-four-errors.rs", "I want to find this!");
}
```
Pass tests are considered to succeed if they compile successfully and have a
`main` function that does not panic when the compiled binary is executed.

[§](https://docs.rs#details)Details

That’s the entire API.

[§](https://docs.rs#workflow)Workflow

There are two ways to update the **.stderr* files as you iterate on your
test cases or your library; handwriting them is not recommended.

First, if a test case is being run as compile_fail but a corresponding
**.stderr* file does not exist, the test runner will save the actual
compiler output with the right filename into a directory called *wip* within
the directory containing Cargo.toml. So you can update these files by
deleting them, running `cargo test`, and moving all the files from *wip*
into your testcase directory.

Alternatively, run `cargo test` with the environment variable
`TRYBUILD2=overwrite` to skip the *wip* directory and write all compiler
output directly in place. You’ll want to check `git diff` afterward to be
sure the compiler’s output is what you had in mind.

[§](https://docs.rs#what-to-test)What to test

When it comes to compile-fail tests, write tests for anything for which you care to find out when there are changes in the user-facing compiler output. As a negative example, please don’t write compile-fail tests simply calling all of your public APIs with arguments of the wrong type; there would be no benefit.

A common use would be for testing specific targeted error messages emitted
by a procedural macro. For example the derive macro from the [ ref-cast](https://github.com/dtolnay/ref-cast)
crate is required to be placed on a type that has either

`#[repr(C)]` or
`#[repr(transparent)]` in order for the expansion to be free of undefined
behavior, which it enforces at compile time:```
error: RefCast trait requires #[repr(C)] or #[repr(transparent)]
 --> $DIR/missing-repr.rs:3:10
  |
3 | #[derive(RefCast)]
  |          ^^^^^^^
```
Macros that consume helper attributes will want to check that unrecognized content within those attributes is properly indicated to the caller. Is the error message correctly placed under the erroneous tokens, not on a useless call_site span?

```
error: unknown serde field attribute `qqq`
 --> $DIR/unknown-attribute.rs:5:13
  |
5 |     #[serde(qqq = "...")]
  |             ^^^
```
Declarative macros can benefit from compile-fail tests too. The [ json!](https://docs.rs/serde_json/1.0/serde_json/macro.json.html)
macro from serde_json is just a great big macro_rules macro but makes an
effort to have error messages from broken JSON in the input always appear on
the most appropriate token:

```
error: no rules expected the token `,`
 --> $DIR/double-comma.rs:4:38
  |
4 |     println!("{}", json!({ "k": null,, }));
  |                                      ^ no rules expected this token in macro call
```
Sometimes we may have a macro that expands successfully but we count on it
to trigger particular compiler errors at some point beyond macro expansion.
For example the [ readonly](https://github.com/dtolnay/readonly) crate introduces struct fields that are public
but readable only, even if the caller has a &mut reference to the
surrounding struct. If someone writes to a readonly field, we need to be
sure that it wouldn’t compile:

```
error[E0594]: cannot assign to data in a `&` reference
  --> $DIR/write-a-readonly.rs:17:26
   |
17 |     println!("{}", s.n); s.n += 1;
   |                          ^^^^^^^^ cannot assign
```
In all of these cases, the compiler’s output can change because our crate or one of our dependencies broke something, or as a consequence of changes in the Rust compiler. Both are good reasons to have well conceived compile-fail tests. If we refactor and mistakenly cause an error that used to be correct to now no longer be emitted or be emitted in the wrong place, that is important for a test suite to catch. If the compiler changes something that makes error messages that we care about substantially worse, it is also important to catch and report as a compiler issue.

[§](https://docs.rs#inline-checks)Inline checks

It’s possible to provide a code to compile directly through
`compile_fail_inline` and `pass_inline`. It allows you to have some more
generic checks which can be generated at runtime if needed.

[§](https://docs.rs#sub-string-checks)Sub-string checks

If you need  more control over the stderr check as well, you can take a
look at `compile_fail_check_sub` and `compile_fail_inline_check_sub`.

---

# interpolator - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/interpolator/latest/target-redirect/i686-pc-windows-msvc/interpolator/

## Expand description

Runtime implementation of [ format!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/macro.format.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#stdfmt-compatible-formatting)`std::fmt` compatible formatting

All options but the fill character for alignment is supported
(due to [rust-lang/rfcs#3394](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3394)).

Though the non [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) traits need to be enabled through

[features](https://docs.rs#features).

```
use interpolator::{format, Formattable};
let formatted = format(
    "{value:+05}", // could be dynamic
    &[("value", Formattable::display(&12))]
        .into_iter()
        .collect::<HashMap<_, _>>(),
)?;
assert_eq!(formatted, format!("{:+05}", 12));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#i-iter-format)`i` iter format

The feature `iter` enables an additional format trait `i`, it allows to
format a list of values with a format string and an optional join
expression.

The syntax is `{list:i(the format string, '{}' is the array element)(the join)}`, an empty join can also be omitted `{list:i({})}`. If join is omitted
the format string `{}` can be omitted as well `{list:i}`.

Should you need to use `)` inside your format string or join, you can add `#`
similar to rust’s [raw string](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/tokens.html#raw-string-literals)
(i.e. `#(({}))#`).

It is also possible to only iterate a sub-slice specified through a range
before the format string, i.e. `{list:i1..4}`. For open ranges range
bounds can also be omitted. To index from the end, you can use negative
range bounds.

It is also possible to index a single value by only specifying an `isize``{list:i1}`.

A [ Formattable](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html) implementing iter is created using

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html#method.iter)

`Formattable::iter````
// HashMap macro
use collection_literals::hash;
use interpolator::{format, Formattable};
// Needs to be a slice of references because `Formattable::display` expects a
// reference
let items = [&"hello", &"hi", &"hey"].map(Formattable::display);
let items = Formattable::iter(&items);
let format_str = "Greetings: {items:i..-1(`{}{outside}`)(, )} and `{items:i-1}{outside}`";
assert_eq!(
    format(format_str, &hash!("items" => items, "outside" => Formattable::display(&'!')))?,
    "Greetings: `hello!`, `hi!` and `hey!`"
);
```
See [ format()](https://docs.rs/fn.format.html) and

[for details.](https://docs.rs/fn.write.html)

`write()`[§](https://docs.rs#macros)Macros

To simplify creating contexts, some macros are provided.

- `context!`- `HashMap<&str, Formattable>`- `format()`
- `list!`- `Formattable`- [iter](https://docs.rs/%60i%60-iter-format).
- `iformat!`- `iwrite!`- `format()`- `write()`
- Most of std’s formatting macros are supported with an `i`prefix:

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

By default only [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) is supported, the rest of the

[formatting traits](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/index.html#formatting-traits)can be enabled through the following features.

- `debug`enables- `?`,- `x?`and- `X?`trait specifiers
- `number`enables- `x`,- `X`,- `b`,- `o`,- `e`and- `E`trait specifiers
- `pointer`enables- `p`trait specifiers
- `iter`enables- `i`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros-1)

- [context](https://docs.rs/macro.context.html)
- Creates a context for use with this crate’s `format()``write()`
- [ieprint](https://docs.rs/macro.ieprint.html)
- `eprint!`- `iformat!`
- [ieprintln](https://docs.rs/macro.ieprintln.html)
- `eprintln!`- `iformat!`
- [iformat](https://docs.rs/macro.iformat.html)
- `format()`
- [iprint](https://docs.rs/macro.iprint.html)
- `print!`- `iformat!`
- [iprintln](https://docs.rs/macro.iprintln.html)
- `println!`- `iformat!`
- [iwrite](https://docs.rs/macro.iwrite.html)
- `write()`
- [iwriteln](https://docs.rs/macro.iwriteln.html)
- Like `writeln!``write()`
- [list](https://docs.rs/macro.list.html)
- Creates a list of formattable values, applying th specified traits, or display if without a trait specifier.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Formattable](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html)
- Utility struct holding references to the trait implementation of a value to enable runtime verification and execution of them

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- Error returned by `format()`
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/enum.ParseError.html)- Error
- Error caused by invalid format string
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.Trait.html)
- The trait used to format.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Context](https://docs.rs/trait.Context.html)
- Context for `format`and`write`

---

# interpolator - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/interpolator/latest/target-redirect/x86_64-pc-windows-msvc/interpolator/

## Expand description

Runtime implementation of [ format!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/macro.format.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#stdfmt-compatible-formatting)`std::fmt` compatible formatting

All options but the fill character for alignment is supported
(due to [rust-lang/rfcs#3394](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3394)).

Though the non [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) traits need to be enabled through

[features](https://docs.rs#features).

```
use interpolator::{format, Formattable};
let formatted = format(
    "{value:+05}", // could be dynamic
    &[("value", Formattable::display(&12))]
        .into_iter()
        .collect::<HashMap<_, _>>(),

```

format a list of values with a format string and an optional join
expression.

The syntax is `{list:i(the format string, '{}' is the array element)(the join)}`, an empty join can also be omitted `{list:i({})}`. If join is omitted
the format string `{}` can be omitted as well `{list:i}`.

Should you need to use `)` inside your format string or join, you can add `#`
similar to rust’s [raw string](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/tokens.html#raw-string-literals)
(i.e. `#(({}))#`).

It is also possible to only iterate a sub-slice specified through a range
before the format string, i.e. `{list:i1..4}`. For open ranges range
bounds can also be omitted. To index from the end, you can use negative
range bounds.

It is also possible to index a single value by only specifying an `isize``{list:i1}`.

A [ Formattable](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html) implementing iter is created using

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html#method.iter)

`Formattable::iter````
// HashMap macro
use collection_literals::hash;
use interpolator::{format, Formattable};
// Needs to be a slice of references because `Formattable::display` expects a
// reference
let items = [&"hello", &"hi", &"hey"].map(Formattable::display);
let items = Formattable::iter(&items);
let format_str = "Greetings: {items:i..-1(`{}{outside}`)(, )} and `{items:i-1}{outside}`";
assert_eq!(
    format(format_str, &hash!("items" => items, "outside" => Formattable::display(&'!')))?,
    "Greetings: `hello!`, `hi!` and `hey!`"
);
```
See [ format()](https://docs.rs/fn.format.html) and

[for details.](https://docs.rs/fn.write.html)

`write()`[§](https://docs.rs#macros)Macros

To simplify creating contexts, some macros are provided.

- `context!`- `HashMap<&str, Formattable>`- `format()`
- `list!`- `Formattable`- [iter](https://docs.rs/%60i%60-iter-format).
- `iformat!`- `iwrite!`- `format()`- `write()`
- Most of std’s formatting macros are supported with an `i`prefix:

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

By default only [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) is supported, the rest of the

[formatting traits](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/index.html#formatting-traits)can be enabled through the following features.

- `debug`enables- `?`,- `x?`and- `X?`trait specifiers
- `number`enables- `x`,- `X`,- `b`,- `o`,- `e`and- `E`trait specifiers
- `pointer`enables- `p`trait specifiers
- `iter`enables- `i`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros-1)

- [context](https://docs.rs/macro.context.html)
- Creates a context for use with this crate’s `format()``write()`
- [ieprint](https://docs.rs/macro.ieprint.html)
- `eprint!`- `iformat!`
- [ieprintln](https://docs.rs/macro.ieprintln.html)
- `eprintln!`- `iformat!`
- [iformat](https://docs.rs/macro.iformat.html)
- `format()`
- [iprint](https://docs.rs/macro.iprint.html)
- `print!`- `iformat!`
- [iprintln](https://docs.rs/macro.iprintln.html)
- `println!`- `iformat!`
- [iwrite](https://docs.rs/macro.iwrite.html)
- `write()`
- [iwriteln](https://docs.rs/macro.iwriteln.html)
- Like `writeln!``write()`
- [list](https://docs.rs/macro.list.html)
- Creates a list of formattable values, applying th specified traits, or display if without a trait specifier.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Formattable](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html)
- Utility struct holding references to the trait implementation of a value to enable runtime verification and execution of them

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- Error returned by `format()`
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/enum.ParseError.html)- Error
- Error caused by invalid format string
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.Trait.html)

# interpolator - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/interpolator/latest/target-redirect/interpolator/

## Expand description

Runtime implementation of [ format!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/macro.format.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#stdfmt-compatible-formatting)`std::fmt` compatible formatting

All options but the fill character for alignment is supported
(due to [rust-lang/rfcs#3394](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3394)).

Though the non [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) traits need to be enabled through

[features](https://docs.rs#features).

```
use interpolator::{format, Formattable};
let formatted = format(
    "{value:+05}", // could be dynamic
    &[("value", Formattable::display(&12))]
        .into_iter()
        .collect::<HashMap<_, _>>(),
)?;
assert_eq!(formatted, format!("{:+05}", 12));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#i-iter-format)`i` iter format

The feature `iter` enables an additional format trait `i`, it allows to
format a list of values with a format string and an optional join
expression.

The syntax is `{list:i(the format string, '{}' is the array element)(the join)}`, an empty join can also be omitted `{list:i({})}`. If join is omitted
the format string `{}` can be omitted as well `{list:i}`.

Should you need to use `)` inside your format string or join, you can add `#`
similar to rust’s [raw string](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/tokens.html#raw-string-literals)
(i.e. `#(({}))#`).

It is also possible to only iterate a sub-slice specified through a range
before the format string, i.e. `{list:i1..4}`. For open ranges range
bounds can also be omitted. To index from the end, you can use negative
range bounds.

It is also possible to index a single value by only specifying an `isize``{list:i1}`.

A [ Formattable](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html) implementing iter is created using

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html#method.iter)

`Formattable::iter````
// HashMap macro

// reference

    "Greetings: `hello!`, `hi!` and `hey!`"

```

[for details.](https://docs.rs/fn.write.html)

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

---

# Badges

Source: https://docs.rs/about/badges

Docs.rs no longer has its own badges. Consider using [shields.io](https://shields.io) instead.

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (4c9d2bfe4 2026-07-01)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

---

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

---

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

# smooth_operator_adapter_memory - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-adapter-memory/1.11.1/smooth_operator_adapter_memory/

## Expand description

In-memory [ StorageAdapter](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/adapter/trait.StorageAdapter.html) — the conformance / test baseline.

All OLTP slices (conversations, participants, messages, sessions) live in
`HashMap`s behind a single `RwLock`. The checkpoint and knowledge slices
delegate to smooth-operator’s own [ MemoryCheckpointStore](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-core/0.15.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator_core/checkpoint/struct.MemoryCheckpointStore.html) and

[, which are exactly what the engine expects — so this adapter is a faithful (if non-durable) stand-in for Postgres/DynamoDB.](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-core/0.15.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator_core/knowledge/struct.InMemoryKnowledge.html)

# smooth_operator_ingestion - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-ingestion/1.11.1/smooth_operator_ingestion/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#smooth-operator-ingestion)smooth-operator ingestion

Knowledge **ingestion + connectors** for smooth-operator — the pipeline
that pulls documents from a source, chunks them, embeds them, and stores them
in the [ StorageAdapter](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator/adapter/trait.StorageAdapter.html)
knowledge slice so they are retrievable. This closes feature gap G1 (knowledge
ingestion + connectors), G2 (document chunking pipeline), and G9 (the
connector mock +

`unit`-vs-`external` test split). See `docs/INGESTION.md`.[§](https://docs.rs#shape)Shape

```
Connector::pull ─▶ Chunker::chunk ─▶ Embedder::embed ─▶ KnowledgeBase::ingest
   RawDocument        Vec<Chunk>        Vec<Vec<f32>>        (StorageAdapter
                                                              knowledge slice)
```
- `Connector`- `RawDocument`- `pull(since)`). Built-ins:- `FileConnector`- `WebConnector`- `MockConnector`
- `Chunker`
- `Embedder`- `smooth_operator::embedding`- `DeterministicEmbedder`
- `ingest`- `(doc id, content hash)`via an- `IngestLedger`

[§](https://docs.rs#wiring-example)Wiring example

```
let connector = FileConnector::new("./docs");
let report = ingest(
    &connector,
    &Chunker::default(),
    &DeterministicEmbedder::new(),
    storage.knowledge(),
    IngestOptions::for_org("org-acme"),
)
.await?;
println!("stored {} chunks", report.chunks_stored);
```

- Default embedding dimension (Voyage `voyage-3-large`shape; mirrors smooai’s`knowledge_vectors embedding vector(1024)`).

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Embedder](https://docs.rs/trait.Embedder.html)
- Turn text into dense vectors. Implementations must return one vector per
input string, each of length `Embedder::dim`

# smooth_operator - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator/1.11.1/smooth_operator/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#smooth-operator)smooth-operator

The reference core for smooth-operator — the service layer on top of
[ smooth_operator_core](https://docs.rs/smooai-smooth-operator-core/0.15.0/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/smooth_operator_core/index.html) (the agent engine). It defines three things:

- `domain`- `spec/domain/*.json`. Checkpoints re-use the engine’s- `smooth_operator_core::Checkpoint`
- `adapter`- `StorageAdapter`- `docs/STORAGE.md`). Its checkpoint/knowledge accessors return smooth-operator-core’s own traits so the engine plugs straight in.
- `runtime`- `AgentRuntime`- `Agent`- `Workflow`

It also owns two shared retrieval seams both backends/consumers depend on:
[ embedding](https://docs.rs/embedding/index.html) (the text→vector

[+ the network-free](https://docs.rs/embedding/trait.Embedder.html)

`Embedder`[, the one home for both the Postgres adapter and the ingestion pipeline) and](https://docs.rs/embedding/struct.DeterministicEmbedder.html)

`DeterministicEmbedder`[(the optional post-retrieval](https://docs.rs/rerank/index.html)

`rerank`[stage — feature gap G8).](https://docs.rs/rerank/trait.Reranker.html)

- [access_](https://docs.rs/access_control/index.html)- control
- Document-level access control (feature gap G3).
- [adapter](https://docs.rs/adapter/index.html)
- The `StorageAdapter`seam.
- [agent_](https://docs.rs/agent_config/index.html)- config
- Per-agent behavior config (SMOODEV-590 parity in Rust).
- [auth](https://docs.rs/auth/index.html)
- Authentication + role-based access control (Phase 12).
- [backplane](https://docs.rs/backplane/index.html)
- Connection backplane: the scale-out + event-delivery seam for the WebSocket server.
- [connector_](https://docs.rs/connector_config/index.html)- config
- Connector configuration storage (Phase 12, increment 3).
- [curation](https://docs.rs/curation/index.html)
- Document sets, curation boosting, and query-time metadata filters (feature gap, Phase 11 — “Document sets / curation / boosting”).
- [domain](https://docs.rs/domain/index.html)
- Domain model for smooth-operator.
- [embedding](https://docs.rs/embedding/index.html)
- Text → vector embedding — the shared seam for dense retrieval.
- [gateway_](https://docs.rs/gateway_key/index.html)- key
- Per-org LLM gateway-key resolution: the seam that lets a multi-tenant
deployment bill/scope each org’s turns to its **own**gateway key while a standalone/local server keeps using the single environment key.
- [otp](https://docs.rs/otp/index.html)
- End-user identity verification (OTP) — the seam that lets a host wire a
one-time-code flow behind a public agent’s `end_user`tool auth, while the reference server stays credential-free.
- [rerank](https://docs.rs/rerank/index.html)
- Reranking — the optional post-retrieval reorder stage (feature gap G8).
- [runtime](https://docs.rs/runtime/index.html)
- Minimal `AgentRuntime`that proves smooth-operator consumes smooth-operator.
- [settings](https://docs.rs/settings/index.html)
- Per-org agent settings storage (Phase 12, increment 3).
- [telemetry](https://docs.rs/telemetry/index.html)
- OpenTelemetry GenAI instrumentation for the agent turn.
- [tool_](https://docs.rs/tool_provider/index.html)- provider
- Host-contributed tool injection seam.
- [tools](https://docs.rs/tools/index.html)
- Tools the smooth-operator runtime registers on the smooth-operator-core engine.
- [widget_](https://docs.rs/widget_auth/index.html)- auth
- Embeddable-widget auth: an origin allowlist + public-key `authContext`verification for browser-embedded chat widgets (`<smooth-agent-chat>`).

# stop - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/stop-cli/0.0.2/stop/

## Expand description

Process and system monitoring with structured output.

Provides cross-platform system metrics collection with filtering, sorting, and multiple output formats (JSON, CSV, human-readable).

- [SetPsm](https://docs.rs/struct.SetPsmStorageVersionV2.html)- Storage - Version - V2
- One-shot migration: writes `pallet_psm`’s on-chain storage version to v2. Required because`RemovePallet<PsmName>`(above in the migration tuple) wipes the pallet’s`:__STORAGE_VERSION__:`key, and`InitializePsm`doesn’t re-seed it. Without this, try-runtime’s post-upgrade check sees in-code = 2, on-chain = 0 and panics.

# masl_formatter - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/masl_formatter/1.0.0/masl_formatter/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#masl_formatter)masl_formatter

Canonical source code formatter for `.mdk` files.

Consumes an `masl_ast::Document` and produces formatted MASL source text.
Never modifies semantics. Guarantees idempotency: fmt(fmt(S)) == fmt(S).

See RFC-0019 — Formatter.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [format](https://docs.rs/fn.format.html)
- Format a parsed AST Document back to canonical MASL source text.

All providers implement the `LlmProvider` trait and are registered in
`ProviderRegistry`. The failover manager sits on top and handles

- Modifies the behavior when sending resumption data.

# bridge_hub_test_utils - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bridge-hub-test-utils/0.34.0/bridge_hub_test_utils/

## Expand description

Module contains predefined test-case scenarios for “BridgeHub” `Runtime`s.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [test_](https://docs.rs/test_cases/index.html)- cases
- Module contains predefined test-case scenarios for `Runtime`with bridging capabilities.
- [test_](https://docs.rs/test_data/index.html)- data
- Generating test data, used by all tests.

- [Collator](https://docs.rs/struct.CollatorSessionKeys.html)- Session - Keys

- Basic builder based on balances, collators and pallet_session.

- A set of traits for a minimal parachain runtime, that may be used in conjunction with the

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [assert_](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_metadata.html)- metadata
- [assert_](https://docs.rs/fn.assert_total.html)- total
- [check_](https://docs.rs/fn.check_sane_fees_values.html)- sane_ - fees_ - values
- A helper function for comparing the actual value of a fee constant with its estimated value. The
estimated value can be overestimated (`overestimate_in_percent`), and if the difference to the actual value is below`margin_overestimate_diff_in_percent_for_lowering`, we should lower the actual value.
- [diff_](https://docs.rs/fn.diff_as_percent.html)- as_ - percent
- [ensure_](https://docs.rs/fn.ensure_opened_bridge.html)- opened_ - bridge
- Helper function to open the bridge/lane for `source`and`destination`while ensuring all required balances are placed into the SA of the source.
- [mock_](https://docs.rs/fn.mock_open_hrmp_channel.html)- open_ - hrmp_ - channel
- Helper function which emulates opening HRMP channel which is needed for `XcmpQueue`to pass.
- [open_](https://docs.rs/fn.open_bridge_with_extrinsic.html)- bridge_ - with_ - extrinsic
- Utility for opening bridge with dedicated `pallet_xcm_bridge_hub`’s extrinsic.
- [open_](https://docs.rs/fn.open_bridge_with_storage.html)- bridge_ - with_ - storage
- Utility for opening bridge directly inserting data to the `pallet_xcm_bridge_hub`’s storage (used only for legacy purposes).
- [test_](https://docs.rs/fn.test_header.html)- header
- Get a header for testing.

# aipmc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aipmc/0.0.1/aipmc/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#aipmc-aip-%E6%99%BA%E8%83%BD%E4%BD%93%E4%BA%92%E8%81%94%E5%8D%8F%E8%AE%AE-mcu-%E5%AE%9E%E7%8E%B0)aipmc: AIP 智能体互联协议 MCU 实现

本 crate 是 AIPMC 项目的统一导出层，将所有子模块重新导出，
用户只需引入 `aipmc` 即可使用完整的协议栈功能。

[§](https://docs.rs#%E5%AD%90%E6%A8%A1%E5%9D%97)子模块

| 模块 | crate | 说明 |
|---|---|---|
| `basic` | aipmc-basic | 核心协议库（协议/消息/编解码） |
| `transport` | aipmc-transport | 传输层（UART/WiFi/BLE） |
| [ `esp32`] | aipmc-esp32 | ESP-32 平台适配（需 feature） |
| [ `stm32`] | aipmc-stm32 | STM-32 平台适配（需 feature） |

[§](https://docs.rs#%E4%BD%BF%E7%94%A8%E7%A4%BA%E4%BE%8B)使用示例

```
use aipmc::basic::{AgentCard, AgentSkill, AcpMessage, AcpMethod, AgentCapability};
let agent = AgentCard::new("dev-01", "MyAgent", "A test agent")
    .unwrap()
    .with_capability(AgentCapability::SensorRead)
    .unwrap()
    .with_skill(AgentSkill::new("temp", "ReadTemp", "Read temperature").unwrap())
    .unwrap();
let msg = AcpMessage::with_payload(AcpMethod::Initialize, 0, b"hello").unwrap();
let encoded = msg.encode().unwrap();
let decoded = AcpMessage::decode(&encoded).unwrap();
assert_eq!(decoded.session_id, 0);
```

---

# aipmc_stm32 - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aipmc-stm32/0.0.1/aipmc_stm32/

[§](#aipmc-stm32-aip-%E6%99%BA%E8%83%BD%E4%BD%93%E4%BA%92%E8%81%94%E5%8D%8F%E8%AE%AE-stm-32-%E5%B9%B3%E5%8F%B0%E9%80%82%E9%85%8D%E5%B1%82)aipmc-stm32: AIP 智能体互联协议 STM-32 平台适配层

提供 STM-32 系列芯片的硬件抽象层（HAL），封装 UART/SPI 初始化、
GPIO 控制等平台特定功能，使上层协议栈无需关注硬件细节。

[§](#%E6%94%AF%E6%8C%81%E7%9A%84%E8%8A%AF%E7%89%87%E7%B3%BB%E5%88%97)支持的芯片系列

| Feature | 芯片系列 |
|---|
| `stm32f4` | STM32F4xx |
| `stm32h7` | STM32H7xx |
| `stm32l4` | STM32L4xx |
| `stm32g4` | STM32G4xx |

[§](#%E5%BD%93%E5%89%8D%E7%8A%B6%E6%80%81)当前状态

骨架实现，待对接 `stm32-hal` 后完善。

---

# interpolator 0.5.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/interpolator/0.5.0

# interpolator

Runtime implementation of `format!`.

`format`

Runtime version of `format!`.

Takes a string and a context, containing `Formattable` values, returns a
string.

```
use HashMap;
use ;
let formatted = format
.unwrap;
assert_eq!;
```
`write`

Runtime version of `write!`.

Takes a mutable `Write` e.g. `&mut String`, a format string and a context,
containing `Formattable` values.

```
use HashMap;
use ;

let mut buf = Stringnew;
write
.unwrap;

assert_eq!;
```
`i` iter format

The feature `iter` enables an additional format trait `i`, it allows to
format a list of values with a format string and an optional join
expression.

The syntax is `{list:i(the format string, '{}' is the array element)(the join)}`, an empty join can also be omitted `{list:i({})}`. If join is omitted
the format string `{}` can be omitted as well `{list:i}`.

Should you need to use `)` inside your format string or join, you can add `#`
similar to rust's [raw string](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/tokens.html#raw-string-literals)
(i.e. `#(({}))#`).

It is also possible to only iterate a sub-slice specified through a range
before the format string, i.e. `{list:i1..4}`. For open ranges range
bounds can also be omitted. To index from the end, you can use negative
range bounds.

It is also possible to index a single value by only specifying an `isize`
`{list:i1}`.

A `Formattable` implementing iter is created using `Formattable::iter`:

```
// HashMap macro
use hash;
use ;
// Needs to be a slice of references because `Formattable::display` expects a
// reference
let items = .map;
let items = iter;
let format_str = "Greetings: {items:i..-1(`{it}`)(, )} and {items:i-1..(`{it}`)}";
assert_eq!;
# return Ok::
```
# Features

By default only `Display` is supported, the rest of the
[formatting traits](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/index.html#formatting-traits)
can be enabled through the following features.

- `debug`enables- `?`,- `x?`and- `X?`trait specifiers
- `number`enables- `x`,- `X`,- `b`,- `o`,- `e`and- `E`trait specifiers
- `pointer`enables- `p`trait specifiers
- `iter`enables- `i`trait specifier

---

# interpolator 0.5.0 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/interpolator/0.5.0/source/

#
                    interpolator 0.5.0

                runtime format strings, fully compatible with std's macros

# interpolator - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/interpolator/0.5.0/target-redirect/i686-pc-windows-msvc/interpolator/

## Expand description

Runtime implementation of [ format!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/macro.format.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#stdfmt-compatible-formatting)`std::fmt` compatible formatting

All options but the fill character for alignment is supported
(due to [rust-lang/rfcs#3394](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3394)).

Though the non [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) traits need to be enabled through

[features](https://docs.rs#features).

```
use interpolator::{format, Formattable};
let formatted = format(
    "{value:+05}", // could be dynamic
    &[("value", Formattable::display(&12))]
        .into_iter()
        .collect::<HashMap<_, _>>(),
)?;
assert_eq!(formatted, format!("{:+05}", 12));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#i-iter-format)`i` iter format

The feature `iter` enables an additional format trait `i`, it allows to
format a list of values with a format string and an optional join
expression.

The syntax is `{list:i(the format string, '{}' is the array element)(the join)}`, an empty join can also be omitted `{list:i({})}`. If join is omitted
the format string `{}` can be omitted as well `{list:i}`.

Should you need to use `)` inside your format string or join, you can add `#`
similar to rust’s [raw string](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/tokens.html#raw-string-literals)
(i.e. `#(({}))#`).

It is also possible to only iterate a sub-slice specified through a range
before the format string, i.e. `{list:i1..4}`. For open ranges range
bounds can also be omitted. To index from the end, you can use negative
range bounds.

It is also possible to index a single value by only specifying an `isize``{list:i1}`.

A [ Formattable](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html) implementing iter is created using

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html#method.iter)

`Formattable::iter````
// HashMap macro
use collection_literals::hash;
use interpolator::{format, Formattable};
// Needs to be a slice of references because `Formattable::display` expects a
// reference
let items = [&"hello", &"hi", &"hey"].map(Formattable::display);
let items = Formattable::iter(&items);
let format_str = "Greetings: {items:i..-1(`{}{outside}`)(, )} and `{items:i-1}{outside}`";
assert_eq!(
    format(format_str, &hash!("items" => items, "outside" => Formattable::display(&'!')))?,
    "Greetings: `hello!`, `hi!` and `hey!`"
);
```
See [ format()](https://docs.rs/fn.format.html) and

[for details.](https://docs.rs/fn.write.html)

`write()`[§](https://docs.rs#macros)Macros

To simplify creating contexts, some macros are provided.

- `context!`- `HashMap<&str, Formattable>`- `format()`
- `list!`- `Formattable`- [iter](https://docs.rs/%60i%60-iter-format).
- `iformat!`- `iwrite!`- `format()`- `write()`
- Most of std’s formatting macros are supported with an `i`prefix:

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

By default only [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) is supported, the rest of the

[formatting traits](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/index.html#formatting-traits)can be enabled through the following features.

- `debug`enables- `?`,- `x?`and- `X?`trait specifiers
- `number`enables- `x`,- `X`,- `b`,- `o`,- `e`and- `E`trait specifiers
- `pointer`enables- `p`trait specifiers
- `iter`enables- `i`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros-1)

- [context](https://docs.rs/macro.context.html)
- Creates a context for use with this crate’s `format()``write()`
- [ieprint](https://docs.rs/macro.ieprint.html)
- `eprint!`- `iformat!`
- [ieprintln](https://docs.rs/macro.ieprintln.html)
- `eprintln!`- `iformat!`
- [iformat](https://docs.rs/macro.iformat.html)
- `format()`
- [iprint](https://docs.rs/macro.iprint.html)
- `print!`- `iformat!`
- [iprintln](https://docs.rs/macro.iprintln.html)
- `println!`- `iformat!`
- [iwrite](https://docs.rs/macro.iwrite.html)
- `write()`
- [iwriteln](https://docs.rs/macro.iwriteln.html)
- Like `writeln!``write()`
- [list](https://docs.rs/macro.list.html)
- Creates a list of formattable values, applying th specified traits, or display if without a trait specifier.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Formattable](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html)
- Utility struct holding references to the trait implementation of a value to enable runtime verification and execution of them

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Error](https://docs.rs/enum.Error.html)
- Error returned by `format()`
- [Parse](https://docs.rs/enum.ParseError.html)- Error
- Error caused by invalid format string
- [Trait](https://docs.rs/enum.Trait.html)
- The trait used to format.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Context](https://docs.rs/trait.Context.html)
- Context for `format`and`write`

(i.e. `#(({}))#`).

before the format string, i.e. `{list:i1..4}`. For open ranges range
bounds can also be omitted. To index from the end, you can use negative
range bounds.

It is also possible to index a single value by only specifying an `isize``{list:i1}`.

A [ Formattable](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html) implementing iter is created using

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html#method.iter)

`Formattable::iter````
// HashMap macro
use collection_literals::hash;
use interpolator::{format, Formattable};
// Needs to be a slice of references because `Formattable::display` expects a
// reference
let items = [&"hello", &"hi", &"hey"].map(Formattable::display);
let items = Formattable::iter(&items);
let format_str = "Greetings: {items:i..-1(`{}{outside}`)(, )} and `{items:i-1}{outside}`";
assert_eq!(
    format(format_str, &hash!("items" => items, "outside" => Formattable::display(&'!')))?,
    "Greetings: `hello!`, `hi!` and `hey!`"
);
```
See [ format()](https://docs.rs/fn.format.html) and

[for details.](https://docs.rs/fn.write.html)

`write()`[§](https://docs.rs#macros)Macros

To simplify creating contexts, some macros are provided.

- `context!`- `HashMap<&str, Formattable>`- `format()`
- `list!`- `Formattable`- [iter](https://docs.rs/%60i%60-iter-format).
- `iformat!`- `iwrite!`- `format()`- `write()`
- Most of std’s formatting macros are supported with an `i`prefix:

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

By default only [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) is supported, the rest of the

[formatting traits](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/index.html#formatting-traits)can be enabled through the following features.

- `debug`enables- `?`,- `x?`and- `X?`trait specifiers
- `number`enables- `x`,- `X`,- `b`,- `o`,- `e`and- `E`trait specifiers
- `pointer`enables- `p`trait specifiers
- `iter`enables- `i`

- Like `writeln!``write()`

- Creates a list of formattable values, applying th specified traits, or display if without a trait specifier.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

# interpolator - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/interpolator/0.5.0/interpolator/index.html

## Expand description

Runtime implementation of [ format!](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/macro.format.html).

[§](https://docs.rs#stdfmt-compatible-formatting)`std::fmt` compatible formatting

All options but the fill character for alignment is supported
(due to [rust-lang/rfcs#3394](https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/3394)).

Though the non [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) traits need to be enabled through

[features](https://docs.rs#features).

```
use interpolator::{format, Formattable};
let formatted = format(
    "{value:+05}", // could be dynamic
    &[("value", Formattable::display(&12))]
        .into_iter()
        .collect::<HashMap<_, _>>(),
)?;
assert_eq!(formatted, format!("{:+05}", 12));
```
[§](https://docs.rs#i-iter-format)`i` iter format

The feature `iter` enables an additional format trait `i`, it allows to
format a list of values with a format string and an optional join
expression.

The syntax is `{list:i(the format string, '{}' is the array element)(the join)}`, an empty join can also be omitted `{list:i({})}`. If join is omitted
the format string `{}` can be omitted as well `{list:i}`.

Should you need to use `)` inside your format string or join, you can add `#`
similar to rust’s [raw string](https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/tokens.html#raw-string-literals)
(i.e. `#(({}))#`).

It is also possible to only iterate a sub-slice specified through a range
before the format string, i.e. `{list:i1..4}`. For open ranges range
bounds can also be omitted. To index from the end, you can use negative
range bounds.

It is also possible to index a single value by only specifying an `isize``{list:i1}`.

A [ Formattable](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html) implementing iter is created using

[:](https://docs.rs/struct.Formattable.html#method.iter)

`Formattable::iter````
// HashMap macro
use collection_literals::hash;
use interpolator::{format, Formattable};
// Needs to be a slice of references because `Formattable::display` expects a
// reference
let items = [&"hello", &"hi", &"hey"].map(Formattable::display);
let items = Formattable::iter(&items);
let format_str = "Greetings: {items:i..-1(`{}{outside}`)(, )} and `{items:i-1}{outside}`";
assert_eq!(
    format(format_str, &hash!("items" => items, "outside" => Formattable::display(&'!')))?,
    "Greetings: `hello!`, `hi!` and `hey!`"
);
```
See [ format()](https://docs.rs/fn.format.html) and

[for details.](https://docs.rs/fn.write.html)

`write()`[§](https://docs.rs#macros)Macros

To simplify creating contexts, some macros are provided.

- `context!`- `HashMap<&str, Formattable>`- `format()`
- `list!`- `Formattable`- [iter](https://docs.rs/%60i%60-iter-format).
- `iformat!`- `iwrite!`- `format()`- `write()`
- Most of std’s formatting macros are supported with an `i`prefix:

[§](https://docs.rs#features)Features

By default only [ Display](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/fmt/trait.Display.html) is supported, the rest of the

[formatting traits](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/fmt/index.html#formatting-traits)can be enabled through the following features.

- `debug`enables- `?`,- `x?`and- `X?`trait specifiers
- `number`enables- `x`,- `X`,- `b`,- `o`,- `e`and- `E`trait specifiers
- `pointer`enables- `p`trait specifiers
- `iter`enables- `i`

## Macros[§](https://docs.rs#macros-1)

- `write()`

[132](https://docs.rs#132)/// Runtime version of [`format!`].
[133](https://docs.rs#133)///
[134](https://docs.rs#134)/// Takes a string and a context, containing [`Formattable`] values, returns a
[135](https://docs.rs#135)/// string.
[136](https://docs.rs#136)///
[137](https://docs.rs#137)/// ```
[138](https://docs.rs#138)/// # use std::collections::HashMap;
[139](https://docs.rs#139)/// use interpolator::{format, Formattable};
[140](https://docs.rs#140)///
[141](https://docs.rs#141)/// let formatted = format(
[142](https://docs.rs#142)///     "{value:+05}", // could be dynamic
[143](https://docs.rs#143)///     &[("value", Formattable::display(&12))]
[144](https://docs.rs#144)///         .into_iter()
[145](https://docs.rs#145)///         .collect::<HashMap<_, _>>(),
[146](https://docs.rs#146)/// )
[147](https://docs.rs#147)/// .unwrap();
[148](https://docs.rs#148)///
[149](https://docs.rs#149)/// assert_eq!(formatted, format!("{:+05}", 12));
[150](https://docs.rs#150)/// ```
[151](https://docs.rs#151)///
[152](https://docs.rs#152)/// # Errors
[153](https://docs.rs#153)///
[154](https://docs.rs#154)/// It will return an error if the specified format string has invalid syntax,
[155](https://docs.rs#155)/// the type doesn't implement the expected trait, or the formatting itself
[156](https://docs.rs#156)/// failed.
[157](https://docs.rs#157)///
[158](https://docs.rs#158)/// For more details have a look at [`Error`] and [`ParseError`].
[159](https://docs.rs#159)pub fn format(format: &str, context: &impl Context) -> Result<String> {
[160](https://docs.rs#160)    let mut out = String::with_capacity(format.len());
[161](https://docs.rs#161)    write(&mut out, format, context)?;
[162](https://docs.rs#162)    Ok(out)
[163](https://docs.rs#163)}
[164](https://docs.rs#164)

[204](https://docs.rs#204)/// containing [`Formattable`] values.
